# Squeeze Out the Duplicates — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/two-pointers/remove-duplicates-sorted.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Two Pointers** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array/)

Given a sorted array, remove the duplicates in place so each value appears once, keeping the original order, and return the array truncated to the values that remain.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4, sorted non-decreasing
- -100 <= nums[i] <= 100
- sortedness is the whole gift: duplicates are always ADJACENT, so a value only has to be compared with the one before it
- in place — the survivors must end up at the front of the same array

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [1, 1, 2]` | `[1, 2]` | — |
| `nums = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]` | `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]` | — |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. Because the array is sorted, a duplicate is always sitting next to its twin.
2. One index reads, one index marks where the next survivor belongs.
3. Write only when the value differs from the last one written.

</details>

---

## 1. Build a distinct copy

Walk the array collecting values that differ from the last one collected, into a new list.

```python
def remove_duplicates(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out: list[int] = []
    for x in nums:
        if not out or out[-1] != x:
            out.append(x)
    return out
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] removeDuplicates(int[] nums) {
    int[] out = new int[nums.length];
    int size = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (size == 0 || out[size - 1] != x) {
            out[size] = x;
            size++;
        }
    }
    return Arrays.copyOf(out, size);
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> removeDuplicates(const vector<int>& nums) {
    vector<int> out;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (out.empty() || out.back() != x) out.push_back(x);
    }
    return out;
}
```

</details>

---

## 2. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Collecting the distinct values into a set loses the ordering the input handed you and spends memory to rebuild it. Sortedness means a duplicate is always adjacent, so one comparison against the previous survivor is enough — no set, no re-sorting, no extra array.

Keep a write index one past the last survivor. Read forward; whenever the current value differs from the value at the last written slot, it is new, so write it and advance. Because the array is sorted, differing from the previous survivor is the same as being new — that equivalence is what makes the single comparison sufficient. The first element is always a survivor, so the walk starts from the second.

```python
def remove_duplicates(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    if not nums:
        return []
    write = 1
    for read in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != nums[write - 1]:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return nums[:write]
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] removeDuplicates(int[] nums) {
    if (nums.length == 0) return new int[0];
    int write = 1;
    for (int read = 1; read < nums.length; read++) {
        if (nums[read] != nums[write - 1]) {
            nums[write] = nums[read];
            write++;
        }
    }
    return Arrays.copyOf(nums, write);
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> removeDuplicates(vector<int> nums) {
    if (nums.empty()) return {};
    int write = 1;
    for (int read = 1; read < (int)nums.size(); read++) {
        if (nums[read] != nums[write - 1]) {
            nums[write] = nums[read];
            write++;
        }
    }
    nums.resize(write);
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Build a distinct copy | O(n) time · O(n) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(1) space | Collecting the distinct values into a set loses the ordering the input handed you and spends memory to rebuild it. Sortedness means a duplicate is always adjacent, so one comparison against the previous survivor is enough — no set, no re-sorting, no extra array. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def remove_duplicates_build_a_distinct_copy(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out: list[int] = []
    for x in nums:
        if not out or out[-1] != x:
            out.append(x)
    return out


def remove_duplicates_the_one_to_remember(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    if not nums:
        return []
    write = 1
    for read in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != nums[write - 1]:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return nums[:write]

APPROACHES = [
    remove_duplicates_build_a_distinct_copy,
    remove_duplicates_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# a run of three or more equal values, so the writer must fall several places behind the reader — [0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4]; plus an array with no duplicates at all
CASES = [
    lambda: ([1,1,2],),
    lambda: ([0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4],),
    lambda: ([1],),
    lambda: ([1,2,3],),
    lambda: ([2,2,2],),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<41} -> {answers}")
```
